messages.subject: Using the library to get index values for non-square plant distributions
messages.subject_clean: Using the library to get index values for non-square plant distributions
messages.body_plain:
Hello

I have been checking the tutorials for this library and found them to be really good, but I got an issue when trying to work with and irragular crop image. I'm working with an Oil palm image and this crop doesn't have an square or rectangle plant distribution but triangle (for higher plant density per ha), I have been able to count the plants but I can't get any other data like index values. I would like to know if there is any way that I can use this library to get index values from an image of something like this.

Thank you in advance for your support and for letting me participate in this forum

messages.body_plain:
Hey there,

Thanks for asking us... It will be great to see an example like a print from your original image (good resolution is not necessarily).

You can draw different shape files using the function fieldPolygon(). You can draw your polygons (any shape necessary) selecting regions where you want to extract vegetation indices. Here is some more information: https://github.com/OpenDroneMap/FIELDimageR#P15

You also can draw your shapefile using QGIS and import it to R to extract information (item 4 in this link https://github.com/OpenDroneMap/FIELDimageR#P20).

Hope it helps...!

All the best,
Filipe

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for sharing the images. I might be mistaken, but it looks like you can use the fieldRotate function to reorient the plots into a rectangle: https://github.com/OpenDroneMap/FIELDimageR#3-rotating-the-image

For removing soil where the background is green, I suggest trying a range of indices to observe which best differentiates between soil and the tree canopy. To test many indices at once you can use the fieldIndex function:

indices <- fieldIndex(imgstack, Red=1, Green=2, Blue=3, index=c("BI", "BIM", "SCI", "GLI", "HI", "NGRDI", "SI", "VARI", "HUE", "BGI"))

If you have multispectral data with RedEdge and/or Near-Infrared (NIR) channels, you can also include the additional indices: PSRI, NDVI, GNDVI, RVI, NDRE, TVI, CVI, CIG, CIRE, DVI, EVI

Best,
Noah

messages.subject: Estimative of plant height
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Filipe. How are you?
I have a question about use of images to estimate the plants height.
I need to estimate simple images, from a smartphone. Basicly, we have a sequence of images of plants in tubets and i need to difference one by one, with the height like a parameter.
Can i use the FIELDimageR to this or i can't to extract that information with a simple camera or smartphone?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: Estimative of plant height
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

We calculate plant height based on the Digital Surface Model (DSM), which is one output from ortho mosaicing. In this case, we are using the altitude information collected during the drone imagery. Also, there is the overlap methodology during the drone flights (e.g., 80% overlap) that helps the software have an idea about the depth and estimate better the pixel altitude. There is more information in this link: https://github.com/OpenDroneMap/FIELDimageR#P10

I am not sure about cellphones, as far as I know, it is not possible with one single image from your phone. You need to investigate if each pixel has geographic coordinates (latitude, longitude, and altitude) to help you get the DSM.

Hope it helps...!

All the best,
Filipe

> > Just as another tip. Despite this empirical approach solving almost
> > all cases is possible to obtain a thresholding value by some criteria
> > decision like Otsu’s multilevel thresholding method (MOM). The
> > autothresholdr package does it, but index values must be discretized.
> > For example for an NDVI raster:
> >
> > land_ndvi_F <- round(land_ndvi*100,0)
> >
> > # Percentile Otsu’s multilevel thresholding method (MOM)
> > MOM<-auto_thresh(
> > int_arr=values(land_ndvi_F),
> > method="Percentile",
> > ignore_black = FALSE,
> > ignore_white = FALSE,
> > ignore_na = TRUE
> > )
> > MOM
> > [1] 33
> > or 0.33 in real NDVI data scale.
> >
> > Best wishes,
> > Alexandre

Normally, plotting the histogram helps to find the best clipping point (between pics of histogram bars)

> > >
> > > Image<- stack("Image.tif")
> > >

> > >

> > >
